title: How do we deal with more games than players?
author: remorej
selftext: With the flood of custom ai-generated games, how do you people deal with the fact that offer has finally outpaced demand? Do you just accept that you are building a game for yourself? Do you have actual strategies that work and to attract players?

comments.author: robhanz
comments.body:
Make better games.

As of 11/4/26, AI can make good prototypes/tech demos.  Turning that into an actually good game takes a lot more guidance and refinement.

replies.author: metagrue
replies.body: Apparently it can also do lazy posts.

replies.author: robhanz
replies.body:
Nah, bro, my post was 100% artisanal humanslop.

And frankly it's the answer.  As AI gets better, the ability to one-shot a game will become ubiquitous, plus services like AstroCade that make it available to anyone.

The only answer is really "make better games", and if there was a secret sauce for that, every game company on the planet would want it.

That said, there's tons of resources on how to make better games that get into the design aspects of it, rather than the technical parts of it (and knowing the technical bits is useful, even with AI).

comments.author: delicious_pubes
comments.body:
Sure, discovery is worse, but there was already more games than demand. The difference now is that AI has enabled millions of people with no game design experience the ability to attempt to design a game. For all the things AI does well today, it is absolute dogshit at the parts that matter most to players.

It is a great tool but it’s also a mediocrity amplifier.

comments.author: ParkInsider
comments.body:
Did some napkin math, not answering your question. There are 30,000 minutes of YT content created every minute, which are viewed an average of 50 times. So 1.5M minutes of content per minute.

Humanity has approximately 692,000 million minutes of free time per minute.

So YouTube fills around 25/100,000th of humanity's free time.

Steam releases around 50 games per day, so 1,000 hours of new gameplay per day, 45 minutes per minute, give or take. 

Approximately 1/700th of what YouTube adds.

There's still room to grow.

comments.author: Tem_Apples
comments.body:
Supply has absolutely not outpaced demand. People don't demand low quality games made in a couple hundred hours by one dude. 

The biggest shift so far is that entering the market is extremely trivial now. Making big, very high quality, well balanced games is just not that easy. You see all these "I made X clone in 8 days" and the 1 minute demo looks flawless but guaranteed when you play it, it's a buggy mess with no attention to detail.

comments.author: Neither_Berry_100
comments.body:
Steam got like 20k games last year and is on track to hit 24k this year from what I have read. That isn't more games than players. Not even close.

I think AI game dev is fundamentally lacking. Making games is already very hard. Your chances vibe coding are probably much worse. Maybe not for a small success. But a vibe coded game cannot become a big genre defining hit. And you can't expect much without serious effort. And skills.

comments.author: Sorrytokeepyouwaitin
comments.body: Find a niche! ask players what types of games are their dream games and go from there. Life simulators that are actually good and have novel ideas instead of being farming sims are a big niche. Same with dress up games that have goals like the style savvy games. I bet if you made a dress up game crossed with a life simulator and added one more novel aspect to it people would love it! You can’t just make what you enjoy and expect people to run to it. You gotta study niches.
